title: Treatment Planning Software for Mental Health: A Demo Guide
summary: Evaluate treatment planning software for mental health with a sample plan. Test signatures, review dates and what billing can verify for an earlier visit.
body_markdown:
Clinicians use treatment planning software for mental health to document a patient's goals and how they will work toward them. A group practice should expect it to show the current goal at each visit and preserve earlier signed plans for billing review. Test both tasks with the same sample plan.


Start with a question that has held up a claim: which goal was the therapist treating on the visit date? Have a covering therapist and a biller answer it from the record.

## What should treatment planning software for mental health carry forward?


A covering therapist needs to know what the patient wants to change and how they agreed to measure progress. The signed plan should give the therapist a starting point for the next session.


### What belongs in the signed plan?


Choose a sample plan with a goal the patient could recognize in daily life. In this example, the patient wants to get through a work meeting without leaving when someone asks them to speak.


- **Assessed need:** The patient describes leaving meetings early for fear of scrutiny. The clinician records how those absences affect the patient's work.
- **Diagnosis:** The clinician explains how the assessment supports a diagnosis of social anxiety disorder.
- **Measurable goal:** The patient chooses to stay through a regular team meeting. The clinician and patient will track which meetings the patient attends from start to finish.
- **Intervention:** The therapist and patient agree to practice speaking briefly in a meeting through gradual exposure.
- **Review date:** The clinician sets a date to review meeting attendance with the patient and decide whether to adjust the goal.


### What should the next note show?


In the meeting example, the therapist might rehearse answering a question with the patient. The session note describes what they practiced and how the patient responded. If the patient has yet to try it at work, the therapist records that distinction.


Ask a covering clinician to read the note and explain why rehearsal mattered at this visit. Clinicians call this link from assessed need through treatment and progress the[golden thread of documentation](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/golden-thread-documentation) .


## Where do vague plans delay claims and add after-hours work?


A signature tells billing who signed the plan. Even a signed plan can leave a biller asking what need the visit addressed.


### When does billing need clarification?


Consider a variation on the meeting example. The plan says "reduce anxiety," and the visit note says "practiced answering questions." The biller asks the therapist how that practice addressed the patient's difficulty at work.


If the plan names the meeting goal, the therapist may only need to clarify the note. If the goal is missing, revising the note alone leaves the covering clinician with the same question next week.


Track internal holds separately from payer denials when reviewing[medical necessity documentation](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/medical-necessity-documentation) , the record of why a patient needed the service. An internal hold starts when billing pauses a claim before submission. A denial comes after submission, so counting denials alone misses the time staff spend resolving questions in the clinic.


### Who absorbs correction time?


After a full clinical day, the therapist may need to reopen the intake to explain why they chose an intervention. The biller then checks the clarification before releasing the claim. Count the therapist's evening minutes alongside the biller's follow-up time.


Pick a recurring question that sent a clinician back to the intake. Use it to test whether your staff can resolve the question during a vendor walkthrough.


## What should a vendor show from intake through claim review?


Have your staff run the meeting example in the vendor's system. Give the intake concern to the clinician writing the plan. Ask the presenter to let the rest of the team work from the record without coaching.


### Can a covering therapist find the current goal?


Schedule the follow-up with a therapist who did not write the sample plan. The original clinician knows what "reduce anxiety" means for this patient. The covering therapist needs enough detail to use the plan on its own.


- **Plan approval:** Ask the intake clinician to record the concern and the agreed goal, then put the plan through approval. Note any detail the clinician must enter twice.
- **Scheduled follow-up:** Have the covering therapist open the visit from their usual schedule. Ask them to find the current goal.
- **Progress note:** Give the therapist a sample update about the latest meeting. Watch whether they can document progress without retyping the work history.
- **Supervisor review:** Ask a supervisor to find overdue plan reviews across sites. Check whether plans written with different templates appear in the same list.


### Can billing verify the plan for that visit?


Request a goal change after the sample follow-up. The patient can now stay through a meeting and wants to contribute to the discussion. Have the clinician document the new goal and put the revised plan through approval.


Ask billing which goal applied at the earlier visit. Version history can answer that question if it shows the approved plan in effect on the visit date. Have the biller find the attendance goal, identify the approver and show when the speaking goal took effect.


Record each detail someone had to retype and each question staff could only answer with the presenter's help. Choose the handoff that took the most staff time for a limited pilot.

## What should your team check in a demo?


Use the same sample patient for each check. Record what staff can verify on screen and where they need a separate reminder or a call to the treating clinician.


Capability What to ask the vendor to show Why it matters for a group practice


First draft Draft a plan from the sample intake. Show which details the clinician must add. Clinical directors can see how much work remains before signing.


Editing Replace “reduce anxiety” with the patient's meeting goal. Save and reopen the draft. The covering therapist needs the goal the patient actually chose.


Version history Create a revised plan and find the version that applied at the earlier visit. Billing can check a prior claim after the goal changes.


Clinician signature Sign a version, then try editing its text to confirm the signature locks it. Reviewers need to know exactly what the clinician signed.


Reopening a signed plan Reopen a signed version with a reason. Show where a reviewer can find that reason. A supervisor can explain why a signed plan needed correction.


Approval Have a reviewer approve the signed plan and show how staff can verify approval. Teams can distinguish a clinician's signature from completed review.


Patient e-signature Send the plan for e-signature. Sign as the sample patient and check the status. Staff know which patients still need a follow-up.


Review dates Set a review date and find plans due for review across the team. Supervisors can assign follow-ups when clinicians cover for each other.


Plan in the session note Start a note using the current plan. Document what the patient practiced today. The next reader can distinguish the agreed goal from progress at this visit.


## How treatment planning works in mdhub


In mdhub's treatment planning software for mental health, Emma, the[AI clinical assistant](https://www.mdhub.ai/products/emma) , drafts the first plan from the patient chart. The clinician edits and saves the plan in one text body. The plan does not update itself after sessions; clinicians use New Version to revise it and keep earlier versions in the history.


Sign locks that version. Clinicians can reopen it with an optional reason. After Sign and Approve, Send to Patient sends the plan through the patient portal for signature. The status changes from Awaiting patient signature to Patient Signed when the patient signs.


Copy Plan lets clinicians copy the text into another documentation system. Clinicians can choose to use the plan as context for session notes. The care coordinator's Tx Plan skill handles plan follow-ups and reminders.


## How can a clinic test the return before expanding?


Run a pilot with one team while keeping the current record system. Before the team changes how it writes plans, log the questions billing sends back. Use the same definition of a plan-related query throughout the pilot.


### What does rework cost?


Compare periods with similar visit volumes. A quieter schedule can reduce total correction time even when each question takes just as long to resolve.


- **Correction time:** Log active minutes by role, including the biller's initial review, the clinician's reply and the biller's final check.
- **After-hours work:** Mark correction minutes outside scheduled hours. Ask separately about evening plan writing that never generated a billing query.
- **Plan-related holds:** Count claims that billing paused for a plan question. Record the question and when billing released the claim.


For each role, multiply hours avoided by hourly staff cost. Add those amounts and subtract software and setup costs for the same period. Count evening correction minutes only once.


The result estimates the value of recovered staff time. A salaried therapist may earn the same amount but now have time to finish the next review during scheduled hours.


### What can saved time support?


mdhub reports "2+ hours saved daily" for documentation overall. That figure covers work beyond treatment planning. Use your team's measured correction time to estimate the return on this workflow.


[Central Valley Family Therapy](https://www.mdhub.ai/blog-posts/behavioral-health-ai-case-study-central-valley) kept growing its clinician group without growing the front office. Dr. Melissa Tihin said, "It's not replacing the human touch. It's giving us the capacity to actually deliver it."


That experience illustrates staff capacity. It does not establish that treatment planning reduced payer denials. Expand the pilot only if corrections take less time and clinicians can still trace each goal to the visit.

## FAQ


How can billing distinguish a plan-related hold from a coding error?


Record what billing needs to release the claim. A missing link between a visit and the patient's goal calls for clinical clarification. If the record supports the service but the claim lists the wrong code, log a coding correction. Track both reasons if both require work.


How can supervisors standardize reviews without making patient goals generic?


Use the same review questions across sites. Ask what the patient wants to do differently and how the clinician will recognize progress. Let each patient and clinician choose the goal language. Check whether a covering therapist can use it to document the next visit.


What if claim holds fall but therapists still finish plans after hours?


Have a therapist walk through a plan they finished after hours. Separate time spent choosing goals from time spent transferring details the intake already contains. Check whether billing now receives clearer plans because clinicians do extra work before signing. Retest that step with the pilot team before expanding.
